messages.subject: Re: overfitting in DSM
parts:
Rob:

The gamma parameter constraining the wiggliness of the gam fits is
'hardwired' into the call to the gam function that the Distance
interface makes. So this penalty is already imposed by Distance.
Perhaps in a future release of Distance the value of gamma could be
selected by the user, but for the moment 1.4 is the value to which this
argument is set.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: overfitting in DSM
parts:
It's really a problem of fitting gams to spatial data - the problem
occurs when you're extrapolating beyond the range of the data. (It may
not be obvious in terms of (x,y) coords that you're doing this - it may
be some odd or extreme combination of values of other covariates in
those grid cells.) We're developing approaches which provide more
robust extrapolation, but they're not yet available in Distance.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 462e886a5516c28a
messages.subject: Re: overfitting in DSM
parts:
Hi List,

Personally I think the maximum number of degrees of freedom allowed
to a potential explanatory variable should reflect how plausibly
bendy the analyst thinks the relationship could be. The default for
gams is 10 knots, 9 degrees of freedom. Is the response of whales say
to depth for example really likely to be a curve that uses 9 degrees
of freedom? I typically constrain my curves to a maximum of 5 or 6
knots, perhaps more if some purely spatial variable like Lat or Lon
is being used but never now the gam default of 10. This can be
implemented as s(Depth,k=5) in writing the model formula. This still
gives considerable flexibility.

thanks

Charles
